strengths: Novel perspective identifying visual encoders as a key source of LVLM hallucinations, filling an important gap in the literature
Well-motivated identification of three specific issues (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability) with empirical evidence supporting each
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, GPT4o-aided) and three diverse LVLM architectures showing consistent improvements (up to 18% on CHAIR)
Practical training-free approach requiring no model fine-tuning, making it broadly applicable
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating that each component contributes meaningfully to hallucination reduction
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and well-explained methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components; token re-weighting, token subtraction, and contrastive decoding are relatively straightforward techniques whose primary novelty lies in combination
Significant computational overhead of 7.6× compared to vanilla inference (Table 11) raises practical deployment concerns; while faster than OPERA, it is 5× slower than VCD

Questionable design assumptions: (1) Token re-weighting relies on naive captions which may contain hallucinations, yet the claim that hallucinated objects won't match visual tokens is unproven; (2) Noise-averaging approach to capture inherent bias lacks rigorous justification
Inconsistent performance across architectures: InstructBLIP shows limited improvements especially on adversarial POPE split, with paper acknowledging but not addressing Q-Former constraints

Significant performance degradation on knowledge-intensive cognition tasks (Table 10): numerical calculation -15 points, text translation -13 points, suggesting the method may hurt performance when prior knowledge is needed

Limited evaluation methodology: reliance on GPT4o for evaluation without inter-rater metrics, no human evaluation despite hallucination being a quality judgment, modest improvements on detailedness metric suggesting possible information suppression rather than genuine accuracy improvement
Hyperparameter sensitivity with four parameters (α, β, K, l) but insufficient guidance on setting them for new models; same parameters used across diverse architectures despite varying results
Incomplete comparisons with related work: training-required methods (LURE, CLIP-DPO) and other recent hallucination approaches not experimentally compared

Limited failure analysis and ablation of design choices: no systematic analysis of failure modes, no exploration of alternative caption prompts, no justification for specific design decisions (e.g., max pooling in Eq. 7)
Insufficient theoretical justification for design choices connecting identified problems to proposed solutions; Figure 2 shows correlation but not causation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, GPT-4o), models (LLaVA, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL), and datasets (COCO, A-OKVQA, GQA)
Clear problem identification with empirical evidence for three hallucination sources in visual encoders (Figure 2)
Consistent improvements on CHAIR hallucination metric, with up to 18% improvement over previous methods
Training-free approach broadly applicable without requiring model fine-tuning
Thorough ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Tables 6, 12-15)
Good visualizations demonstrating how each component addresses its target issue (Figure 8)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines existing techniques (caption-token similarity re-weighting, noise subtraction, contrastive decoding from VCD) without fundamental innovation

Weak theoretical justification for core claims: (1) token L2 norms as bias is correlational not causal; (2) inherent bias reasoning via noise-derived tokens is circular—no principled explanation for why random noise reliably activates dominant pretraining objects; (3) adversarial attack maximizes similarity to hallucinated naive captions, which appears backwards

Methodological concern with adversarial attack (Eq. 11-15): the attack is designed to match hallucinating model's descriptions rather than expose hallucinations, and no evidence provided that adversarial perturbations correspond to hallucinated objects

Inconsistent improvements across settings: marginal gains on InstructBLIP POPE Random (88.2 vs 89.8), minimal GPT-4o detailedness gains, and degradation on cognition tasks (Table 10), suggesting the method trades off performance
High computational overhead (7.6× slower than vanilla, Table 11) not justified by modest improvements in many metrics

Overclaimed novelty: claims to be 'first to trace to visual encoders' despite recent work [14] already identifying visual attention issues; no controlled experiments isolating visual encoder contribution from LLM
Different decoding strategies across baselines (VCD: sampling, OPERA: beam search, SHIELD: sampling) complicates fair comparison
Naive caption generation (Eq. 4) relies on hallucinating model, potentially propagating errors through re-weighting; assumption that hallucinated objects won't match visual tokens needs validation
Hyperparameter sensitivity requires tuning four parameters (α, β, K, l) with no guidance for new models; ablations show meaningful sensitivity (α: 1.0→2.0)
No failure case analysis or discussion of which hallucination types are not addressed; missing analysis of degradation on cognition tasks
Unclear conceptual distinction between 'statistical bias' and 'inherent bias'—both stem from pretraining data imbalance
Missing code and supplementary materials for reproducibility; missing details on adversarial optimization steps
Limited baseline comparisons: only compares against two training-free methods (VCD, OPERA); no ablations of alternative designs or comparison with other visual feature manipulation approaches

strengths: Novel perspective: First work to systematically attribute LVLM hallucinations to visual encoder biases (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability) rather than just LLM components
Strong empirical validation: Figure 2 provides compelling evidence for all three identified issues through correlation analysis and ablations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, GPT4o), diverse LVLM families (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL), consistent improvements (up to 18% on CHAIR)
Practical training-free approach: Deployable to existing models without retraining, addressing a real operational need
Thorough ablation studies: Clear demonstration of contribution from each module (Table 6, Figures 8)
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations and logical flow of ideas
Improvements on general tasks: Benefits extend beyond hallucination reduction to perception tasks like OCR and Posters (Table 5)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components (token re-weighting via CLIP similarity, noise-based subtraction, contrastive decoding extending VCD) are relatively straightforward; main contribution is their combination

Weak theoretical justification for inherent bias solution: Unclear why averaging noise inputs reveals 'dominant object representations' or how this mechanistically addresses pretraining biases; assumes specific 'dominant object units' without evidence

Circular logic in token re-weighting: Uses hallucinating vanilla LVLM's output as supervision; unproven assumption that hallucinated objects necessarily fail to match visual tokens; no justification for cosine-similarity-to-caption as optimal metric

Cascading use of potentially unreliable naive captions: Naive captions (which may themselves be hallucinations) reused across re-weighting, inherent bias subtraction, and adversarial attack components
Significant computational overhead: 7.6× slower than vanilla (Table 11), substantial practical deployment cost; faster than OPERA but still considerable

Capability degradation on non-hallucination tasks: Performance drops on cognition tasks—numerical calculation (-20%), text translation (-12%), code reasoning (-15%)—and modest detailedness improvements suggest sacrificed descriptiveness

Inconsistent cross-model performance: InstructBLIP shows limited POPE adversarial improvements; different LVLM architectures benefit unequally; same hyperparameters applied across models without justification

Incomplete causal analysis: Limited evidence these three issues are primary hallucination causes; no breakdown of which component addresses which hallucination type; vulnerability not deeply analyzed mechanistically
Parameter sensitivity and tuning burden: Four hyperparameters (α, β, K, l) with sensitivity shown in ablations; K ablation shows non-monotonic behavior; no principled guidance for new models
GPT4o evaluation limitations: Uses proprietary AI system with own biases; may be fooled by plausible hallucinations; detailedness improvements modest, potentially masking capability loss
Limited generalization analysis: Unclear how to adapt SHIELD to different encoder architectures; universal applicability not established; Q-Former in InstructBLIP constrains benefits
Incomplete reproducibility: Code not yet released (promised); GPT4o evaluation depends on proprietary service; missing optimization details for attack tensor generation

strengths: Novel perspective: First systematic study tracing LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders rather than just LLM components, addressing an underexplored direction
Well-motivated problem analysis with clear empirical evidence for three identified issues (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability) demonstrated through Figure 2 analyses

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, AMBER), LVLM families (LLaVA, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL), and recent variants (Qwen2/3), with consistent improvements (18% over OPERA on CHAIR)
Practical training-free approach applicable to existing LVLMs without modification, with promised code release for reproducibility
Thorough analysis including detailed ablations (Table 7), hyperparameter sensitivity studies (Tables 17-21), case studies, and investigation of inherent class-specific biases
Multiple evaluation perspectives: automatic metrics (CHAIR, POPE, MME), attribute-level evaluation (AMBER), GPT-4o-assisted evaluation, and qualitative case studies
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of the framework and module contributions
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead of 2.8× (7.34s vs 2.59s per sample), with most cost from caption generation and adversarial computation, limiting real-world deployment for time-sensitive applications

Naive caption dependency creates potential circularity: token re-weighting relies on a vanilla caption containing hallucinations; the argument that hallucinated objects lack visual grounding is somewhat tautological

Inconsistent improvements across models and tasks: InstructBLIP shows limited POPE improvements due to Q-Former constraints; performance degrades on knowledge-intensive tasks (Table 13), suggesting over-suppression of LLM prior knowledge

Limited theoretical justification: Why noise-derived tokens reveal inherent bias lacks rigorous grounding; connection between adversarial vulnerability and hallucination generation not formally established; choice of cosine similarity loss in Eq. 11 not motivated

Moderate technical novelty: Individual components (caption-based re-weighting, noise averaging, contrastive decoding) are relatively straightforward; novelty lies in combination and problem identification rather than novel techniques
Lack of statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single-run results with unclear stability; some improvements are modest without established significance
Limited evaluation scope: Primarily image captioning and VQA; generalization to other vision-language tasks (visual reasoning, multiple-choice VQA) unclear; only English benchmarks

Incomplete methodology justification: Why residual addition in Eq. 8 versus multiplicative re-weighting (no ablation); K=32 hyperparameter choice lacks convergence analysis; limited guidance for hyperparameter selection on new models
Design choices lacking ablation: Token re-weighting strategy not compared with alternatives; impact of caption quality and prompt sensitivity not thoroughly investigated
Presentation gaps: Some critical experimental details in appendix; recent baselines (VTI, MARINE, DoLa, ICD, TAME) compared only in appendix; inconsistent notation

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, AMBER) and diverse LVLM families (LLaVA, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL), demonstrating broad applicability
Training-free approach requires no model fine-tuning, making it practical for any LVLM
Consistent improvements in hallucination metrics across benchmarks (e.g., 25% reduction on CHAIR for LLaVA-1.5)
Systematic ablation studies clearly show individual module contributions, with hyperparameter sensitivity analysis in appendix
Good reproducibility practices with detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, and code release promised
Novel perspective shifting focus from LLM to visual encoder components as sources of hallucinations
weaknesses: Weak conceptual foundation: The distinction between statistical and inherent bias is fuzzy—both stem from pretraining data imbalance. Figure 2 shows correlations but not causation; the root cause attribution to encoders rather than LLM components is not definitively established

Circular reasoning in token re-weighting: Method generates naive captions from the same hallucinating model, then uses these captions to guide token re-weighting. The claim that hallucinated objects have low visual token similarity is insufficient justification
Residual addition in Eq. (8) amplifies tokens (x^v' = x^v(1+W^v)) rather than redistributing attention, contradicting the stated goal of reducing overemphasized token distortion

Questionable noise-based inherent bias estimation: The theoretical justification that E(random_noise) estimates inherent encoder bias lacks rigor. Why would averaging noise consistently reveal inherent bias patterns?
Significant computational overhead: 7.3 seconds per sample (2.8× slower than vanilla), driven by adversarial tensor optimization, severely limiting real-time applicability

Uneven generalization: InstructBLIP shows minimal improvements (CS 40.4 vs. OPERA 46.4); Qwen-VL underperforms on POPE Adversarial; degradation on cognition tasks suggests trade-offs with general capability

Limited methodological novelty: Individual components (token re-weighting, token subtraction, contrastive decoding) are not novel; contribution is primarily a three-issue framing, which is incremental
Modest GPT-4o evaluation gains: Correctness improvements are more modest (LLaVA-1.5: 4.9→6.2, +25.6%) than CHAIR metrics, raising questions about metric sensitivity and real-world impact
Design choices rely on potentially hallucinated naive captions (token re-weighting, adversarial loss); Section D.2 shows only marginal robustness (80.13 vs. 79.83 F1)
Limited analysis of failure modes and hallucination types not addressed; no investigation of when/why method fails across architectures

strengths: Novel perspective identifying visual encoders as underexplored sources of LVLM hallucinations with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 2) linking token overemphasis, inherent bias, and vulnerability to hallucination rates

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple hallucination types (object/attribute/relation/existence-level), diverse benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE with multiple splits/datasets, MME, AMBER, GPT-4o-aided LLaVA-Bench), and multiple LVLM families with consistent and substantial improvements (18% on CHAIR CS)
Practical training-free approach requiring no model fine-tuning, making it broadly applicable to existing models
Thorough ablation studies validating each component's contribution and hyperparameter sensitivity across multiple dimensions
Well-written paper with clear presentation, informative figures, and extensive supplementary materials supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead (2.8× slowdown: 7.34 vs 2.59 s/sample) primarily from caption generation and adversarial optimization, potentially limiting practical deployment despite being faster than OPERA

Circular dependency in token re-weighting: uses naive caption from vanilla LVLM as reference, risking correlation with baseline hallucinations; while D.2 provides partial analysis, the foundational assumption that hallucinated objects won't match visual tokens deserves deeper theoretical justification

Limited novelty of individual components: token re-weighting via similarity matching is straightforward, token subtraction using noise averaging is intuitive but not novel, and contrastive decoding directly extends VCD; core contribution is primarily problem identification and component combination

Inherent bias estimation via noise inputs lacks rigorous justification for why noise-triggered representations reliably capture pretraining-dominant object biases, and the theoretical connection between noise and inherent bias could be formally established

Generalization limitations: mixed results on some architectures (InstructBLIP POPE improvements are marginal due to Q-Former constraints), and trade-offs with knowledge-heavy tasks (Tables 12-13 show degradation on Celebrity, Scene, Landmark recognition)
Adversarial loss design (Eq. 11 cosine similarity) not principled—alternative objectives not explored; D.3 compares attack methods but not loss functions themselves
Absence of failure case analysis, missing discussion of when SHIELD is ineffective, and no guidance on image/hallucination characteristics that resist mitigation
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests; while 500-image CHAIR samples reduce variance, formal statistical validation would strengthen claims

GPT-4o-aided evaluation introduces dependency on another LLM with potential biases in hallucination detection; 'Correctness' scores are subjective and would benefit from human evaluation or multi-evaluator agreement metrics
